p: a shift over time in the size, age profile or location of a population,
which changes the pool of workers and the pattern of customers that businesses can draw on.
a working arrangement in which employees choose their own start and finish times
as long as they complete an agreed total number of hours.
a labour market in which people take on short-term, task-by-task or freelance work
rather than holding permanent employment with one employer.
the strategic management of an organisation's people, covering recruiting, developing, motivating and retaining them,
so that the workforce helps the organisation achieve its objectives.
forecasting the number and type of workers a business will need in future
and planning how to recruit, train or reduce staff to match that demand.
the movement of people into a country from elsewhere in order to live or work there,
which adds to the labour supply available to its businesses.
the ease with which workers can move between different jobs or industries
or between different geographical areas to take up employment.
the reluctance of employees or managers to accept new ways of working,
usually because they fear losing job security, status or familiar routines.
an organisational system that relies on strict rules and formal procedures
with clearly defined roles and decisions passed through many levels of officials.
authority to make key decisions is held by a small number of senior managers or head office,
so lower-level staff and branches have little say in them.
the line of formal authority running from the top of an organisation to its lowest level,
showing who gives instructions to, and is accountable to, whom.
decision-making authority is passed down to lower levels, branches or departments,
so managers closer to customers and operations can act without head office approval.
removing one or more levels of the management hierarchy,
so the organisation becomes flatter and the remaining managers' spans of control widen.
passing authority for a task or decision down to a subordinate
while the manager remains accountable for the final outcome.
an organisational structure with only a few layers of management
and wide spans of control, which shortens lines of communication.
the count of separate ranks of management and staff
stacked between the top decision maker and the front-line workers.
a structure in which employees belong to both a functional department and a project or product team,
so they answer to two or more managers at the same time.
grouping employees into departments based on the specialist task they perform,
so that people with similar skills work together under one manager.
grouping employees into divisions according to the product or product line they make or sell,
with each division having its own staff for the functions it needs.
grouping employees into units based on the geographical area in which they operate,
so each area can respond to its own customers and local conditions.
a diagram of an organisation's structure
showing job roles, levels of hierarchy and who is accountable to whom.
the formal arrangement of roles, authority and reporting relationships within a business,
which determines how tasks are allocated and how information flows.
a structure in which staff are grouped into temporary teams formed to complete a specific project
and are disbanded or reassigned once it ends.
a structure built on three groups: a small core of permanent key staff, outside contractors, and part-time or temporary workers,
which lets the business flex its labour force as demand changes.
the number of employees a manager directly supervises,
which affects how many levels of hierarchy are needed and how closely staff are managed.
an organisational structure with many layers of management
and narrow spans of control, which allows close supervision but slows communication.
a leadership style in which the leader makes decisions alone
and does not seek or value input from subordinates.
a leadership style in which the leader invites employees to contribute to decisions
and takes their views into account before deciding.
making decisions quickly using gut feeling, instinct and past experience
rather than a lengthy analysis of data.
a leadership style in which the leader gives employees the freedom to make their own decisions
and provides little direction or supervision.
the ability to influence, guide and inspire others
to work willingly towards the achievement of shared goals.
the process of planning, organising, coordinating and controlling resources
in order to achieve organisational objectives efficiently.
a leadership style in which the leader makes the decisions but acts in what they see as the employees' best interests,
explaining their reasons and showing concern for staff welfare.
a decision-making approach based on systematic analysis, evidence and testing of data
in order to reach logical, objective conclusions.
a view that no single leadership style is best,
so the leader adapts their style to the task, the employees and the circumstances.
an appraisal method that gathers opinions on an employee's performance from the many different people they deal with
including managers, colleagues, subordinates and customers, rather than from one supervisor alone.
a formal process of assessing an employee's performance and potential
so that strengths and weaknesses can be identified and decisions on training, rewards or promotion made.
a payment to a worker calculated as a share of the value of the sales they make,
paid in addition to, or instead of, a basic wage.
a theory that people are motivated by three innate psychological needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness,
and that meeting these needs builds intrinsic motivation.
a fall in an employee's enthusiasm and willingness to put effort into their work
which tends to reduce productivity and raise absenteeism.
the ending of an employee's contract by the employer
because of unsatisfactory conduct or performance, rather than because the job is no longer needed.
a scheme that gives employees, or lets them buy, shares in the company they work for,
so they receive a share of its profits through dividends and gain a stake in its success.
giving employees greater authority and freedom to make decisions about their own work
and trusting them to take responsibility for the results.
a theory that employees compare their own effort and rewards with those of colleagues
and become demotivated if they judge the balance to be unfair.
a theory that people are motivated to act when they expect that effort will lead to good performance
and that this performance will lead to an outcome they value.
filling a job vacancy with someone from outside the business,
which brings in new skills and ideas but usually costs more and takes longer than promoting from within.
motivation that comes from outside the individual, through rewards or punishments given by others,
rather than from enjoyment or satisfaction in the work itself.
monetary payments and benefits that employees receive in return for their work,
which are used to attract, motivate and keep staff.
ongoing review of an employee's performance throughout the year,
aimed at giving feedback so they can develop and improve.
benefits that employees receive on top of their basic pay,
given in kind or as perks, which add to the overall value of their employment package.
a theory that job satisfaction and dissatisfaction come from two separate sets of factors:
motivators, which increase satisfaction, and hygiene factors, which prevent dissatisfaction.
in Herzberg's theory, job conditions that do not motivate when they are present
but cause dissatisfaction when they are inadequate.
training given to new employees when they join,
to introduce them to the organisation, their role, their colleagues and its procedures.
filling a vacancy with someone who already works for the organisation, by promotion or transfer,
which is cheaper and faster but limits the range of applicants.
motivation that comes from within a person,
through interest, enjoyment or a sense of achievement in the work itself rather than from external rewards.
adding extra tasks of a similar level to an employee's existing job
so that the work becomes less repetitive.
giving employees more challenging tasks with greater responsibility and decision making,
so that the job becomes more meaningful and motivating.
moving employees between different jobs or tasks at the same level on a regular basis
to reduce boredom and develop a wider range of skills.
the rate at which employees leave an organisation during a given year or other period,
usually measured as the number of leavers divided by the average number employed, as a percentage.
a theory that human needs form a five-level hierarchy, from physiological needs up to self-actualisation,
and that people are motivated to satisfy lower needs before higher ones.
a theory that people develop, through life experience, a dominant need for achievement, affiliation or power,
and that this need shapes what motivates them.
the desire and willingness of a person to put effort into their work,
driven by needs and incentives that determine how hard and for how long they keep trying.
in Herzberg's theory, factors in the job itself that increase satisfaction and encourage employees to work harder,
but whose absence leaves employees neutral rather than dissatisfied.
benefits given to employees that are not direct payments of money
and instead satisfy needs such as recognition, development, status or enjoyment of the work.
training that takes place away from the employee's normal place of work, usually run by outside specialists,
which gives focused learning but means the employee is not producing in the meantime.
training carried out at the employee's own workplace while they perform their normal tasks,
usually guided by an experienced colleague.
pay that varies according to how well an employee or team performs,
measured against agreed targets.
a payment method in which workers are paid for each unit they produce,
so their earnings rise directly with output.
a payment in which part of an employee's pay depends on the profit the business makes,
so staff gain when the firm does well.
the process of attracting suitable applicants for a job vacancy
and selecting the most appropriate candidate to fill it.
a fixed amount paid to an employee for their work, usually quoted annually and paid monthly,
regardless of the exact number of hours worked or output produced.
an appraisal method in which employees rate their own work against agreed objectives
and identify their own strengths and areas needing development.
a formal review of an employee's performance over a set period,
used to make judgements for decisions on pay, promotion or retention.
an approach that seeks to raise productivity by breaking jobs into simple, timed tasks and training workers to do them in the most efficient way,
while motivating them mainly through piece-rate pay.
employees cooperating and combining their different skills and efforts
to achieve a shared goal that individuals might not reach alone.
a payment method in which employees are paid according to the hours they work,
regardless of how much they produce.
the process of developing an employee's skills, knowledge and abilities
so that they can perform their current or future job more effectively.
payment to workers calculated from the hours they work or the units they produce,
typically paid weekly or fortnightly.
charles Handy's classification of organisational cultures into four types named after Greek gods:
Zeus (power), Apollo (role), Athena (task) and Dionysus (person).
the shared beliefs, values and behaviours of the people in an organisation,
which influence how decisions are made and how people act at work.
a culture in which the organisation exists to serve the individuals within it,
who are usually experts working with a high degree of independence.
a culture in which power and decision making are concentrated in a single leader or a small inner circle at the centre,
with few rules and control exercised through personal influence.
a culture built on clearly defined roles, rules and procedures,
where authority comes from a person's position in the hierarchy.
a culture focused on completing specific projects or solving problems
using flexible teams of experts whose influence comes from their expertise rather than their position.
factors that block, distort or delay a message passing between sender and receiver
and so reduce the chance that it is understood as intended.
communication that flows upward from employees to managers,
passing on feedback, ideas and information from the front line.
the process of exchanging information, ideas or instructions between a sender and a receiver
through a medium, with feedback confirming that the message has been understood.
communication that passes along the official channels set out in the organisation's structure
and is usually documented.
communication that takes place outside the official channels,
through casual conversation between employees at any level, and is not usually recorded.
communication that flows downward from senior managers to lower levels,
passing on instructions, decisions and information.
a way of settling a dispute in which an independent third party examines both sides' cases and makes a decision
that the two sides are usually bound to accept.
negotiation between employer representatives and employee representatives, usually a trade union,
to agree pay, hours and working conditions for a group of workers.
a procedure in which an independent third party helps employers and employees reach agreement
by encouraging discussion and suggesting compromises, without imposing a decision.
the involvement of workers in making decisions or shaping how the organisation operates,
ranging from being consulted to having a formal voice at board level.
collective measures taken by employees to put pressure on their employer in a dispute
which disrupt or restrict normal production or service.
a system that gives employees formal representation in how the business is governed,
so that decisions are shared with, rather than imposed on, the workforce.
the relationship between employers and employees or their representatives,
including how disputes, pay and working conditions are negotiated and resolved.
when an employer prevents employees from entering the workplace
to pressure them into accepting the employer's terms in a dispute.
a clause in an agreement in which employees or their union promise not to take strike action for a set period,
usually in return for agreed pay or conditions.
employees refusing to work any hours beyond their contracted hours
while carrying on with their normal hours, to pressure the employer in a dispute.
the loss of a job because the employer no longer needs the position,
not because of the employee's conduct or performance.
an agreement in which an employer recognises only one trade union to represent all its employees
in negotiations over pay and conditions.
a collective refusal by employees to carry out their work
to pressure an employer over a dispute.
an organisation of workers formed to represent their collective interests
by negotiating with employers over pay, conditions and job security.
employees carrying out only the duties set out in their contracts and following every rule strictly,
which slows output without a full strike.
spending on buying or improving non-current assets
that will keep being useful for longer than twelve months.
spending on the everyday running costs of the business
which are used up within the current year, such as wages and utilities.
a wealthy individual who invests their own money in a start-up or small business
in return for part ownership, and often offers advice and contacts as well.
raising finance by collecting small amounts of money from a large number of people
usually through an online platform.
funds obtained from parties outside the firm, such as lenders, investors or suppliers
rather than generated by the business itself.
the first time a company sells its shares to the general public on a stock exchange
which raises share capital and allows the shares to be traded.
money raised from within the business itself
such as the owner's savings, profits kept back or the sale of assets, so no outside party is involved.
paying regular fees to use an asset for an agreed period
while the owner of the asset keeps ownership and the business avoids a large upfront purchase.
money borrowed from a lender such as a bank
which must be repaid with interest over an agreed period.
funds that are repaid over a period longer than a year
and are mostly used to buy non-current assets or pay for expansion.
an organisation that gives very small loans and other financial services
to people and tiny businesses that cannot get finance from traditional banks.
a long-term loan used to buy property
where the property is held as security, so the lender can claim it if repayments are not made.
an arrangement with a bank that lets a business spend more than it has in its account
up to an agreed limit, with interest charged on the amount used.
the owner's own savings put into the business
which is the main starting source of finance for a sole trader.
profit after tax and dividends that the business keeps rather than pays out
so that it can be reinvested in the business.
selling non-current assets the business no longer needs
to raise cash without having to borrow or find new investors.
money raised by selling shares in the company
which gives buyers part ownership and a claim to dividends, and does not have to be repaid.
money raised that is repaid within a year
and is mainly used to cover day-to-day costs and temporary shortages of cash.
an arrangement where a supplier delivers goods now
and allows the business to pay for them later, often after 30 to 90 days.
finance provided by specialist investors to new or fast-growing businesses with high risk and high potential
in exchange for a share of ownership in the business.
costs that can be clearly linked to making a particular product or serving a particular cost centre
such as raw materials and the wages of production workers.
costs that stay the same in total
whatever the level of output, such as rent, in the short run.
costs of running the whole business that cannot be traced to one product
so they are shared across the business, such as management salaries and insurance.
the income a business earns from selling its goods or services
before any costs are taken away.
a separate source of income for a business
such as a product line, a service, a subscription or advertising.
all the costs a business has when producing a given level of output
found by adding together its fixed costs and variable costs.
the full sales income a business earns in a period
found by multiplying the selling price by the quantity sold.
costs that change in total
in direct proportion to the level of output, such as raw materials.
resources that a business owns or controls
which have a money value and are expected to bring benefits in the future.
a financial statement showing what a business owns, owes and is worth
on one particular date, which makes it a snapshot rather than a record over time.
the direct costs of producing the goods or services that were sold in a period
such as materials and production wages, taken from revenue to find gross profit.
cash and items the business expects to convert into cash or consume within twelve months
such as inventory and amounts owed by customers.
debts and other amounts the business owes
that must be paid within a year, such as overdrafts and money owed to suppliers.
the fall in the value of a non-current asset over time
caused by wear, use or becoming out of date, and spread across its useful life as an expense.
a share of a company's profit that is paid out to its shareholders
usually in proportion to the number of shares each person owns.
the part of the business that belongs to its owners
found by taking total liabilities away from total assets.
the set of financial statements a business produces at the end of a period
which includes the profit and loss account and the balance sheet.
the profit left after the cost of sales is taken away from revenue
before other expenses such as rent, wages and marketing are paid.
assets that have value to a business but have no physical form
such as patents, trademarks, copyright and goodwill.
amounts a business owes to other people or organisations
which it will have to pay in cash or in goods and services in the future.
the profit left after all expenses, including overheads, interest and tax, are taken from revenue
which is the amount available to owners or to be kept in the business.
assets that the business plans to keep and use for more than a year
such as buildings, machinery and patents.
debts that the business does not have to repay for more than a year
such as long-term bank loans and mortgages.
the surplus left when a business's total costs are taken away from its total revenue
which rewards owners for the risk of running the business.

term: Profit and loss account (statement of profit or loss)
p: a financial statement setting out a business's revenue, costs and resulting profit
for a trading year or other set accounting period.
the total profit that has been kept in the business over its life
rather than paid out as dividends, shown in the equity section of the balance sheet.
depreciation calculated by taking the same amount off an asset's value every year
found by dividing the cost minus the expected residual value by the asset's useful life.

term: Units of production method of depreciation
p: depreciation calculated from how much an asset is used
so the cost minus residual value is shared across the total units it is expected to produce.
a liquidity ratio that compares current assets, leaving out inventory, with current liabilities
to show whether a business can pay its short-term debts without having to sell its stock.
the total long-term finance used to run a business
found by adding equity and non-current liabilities.
a liquidity ratio that compares a business's current assets with its current liabilities
to show whether it can pay its short-term debts.
gross profit shown as a percentage of revenue
which shows how much is made from each dollar of sales after the direct costs of making them.
how easily an asset can be turned into cash without losing value
which decides whether a business can pay its short-term debts when they fall due.
ratios that compare a business's short-term assets with its short-term debts
to show whether it can meet payments as they fall due.
net profit shown as a percentage of revenue
which shows how much profit is kept from each dollar of sales after all costs.
how successful a business is at earning profit
when compared with its sales or with the resources it has used.
ratios that compare a business's profit with its sales or its capital
to show how well it turns its activity into profit.
a method of comparing figures from the final accounts as ratios
so that performance can be judged over time or against competitors.
operating profit, found before interest and tax are deducted, divided by capital employed and written as a percentage
which shows how well the finance invested in the business earns a profit.
a legal process that a person or business enters when it can no longer pay its debts
in which a court oversees how assets are used to repay creditors.
how many days, on average, a business takes to pay its suppliers
which shows how long it makes use of supplier credit before cash leaves the business.
how many days, on average, customers take to settle what they owe the business
which shows how fast credit sales become cash.
ratios that show how well a business uses its resources
such as its stock, its borrowing, and the credit it gives and receives.
the share of a firm's long-term finance that comes from borrowing
which shows how heavily it relies on debt instead of owners' funds.
the position of being unable to pay debts on time
because liabilities exceed assets or there is too little cash available.
the number of times a business sells and replaces its average stock in a period
which shows how quickly inventory is moving.
money coming into and going out of a business during an accounting period
which decides whether it can pay its bills when they are due.
a prediction of the cash a business expects to receive and pay out
over a future period, which shows the expected cash balance at the end of each period.
money received by a business
from sources such as sales, loans and investment.
money paid out by a business
for items such as wages, supplies, rent and loan repayments.
the cash a business has at the end of a period
found by adding net cash flow to the opening balance.
how much cash and near-cash assets a business has available
compared with the short-term payments it has to make.
the difference between cash inflows and cash outflows in a period
which is positive when more cash comes in than goes out.
the cash a business has at the start of a period
which is the same as the closing balance of the previous period.
the funds available for the business's day-to-day running
found by taking current liabilities away from current assets.
the average annual profit from an investment divided by its initial cost and expressed as a percentage
which lets projects be compared with each other or with a target return.
the interest rate used to convert future cash flows into their value today
which reflects the return the business could earn elsewhere and the risk involved.
the use of quantitative and qualitative techniques to judge an investment project
to help a business decide whether to go ahead with it.
the total of a project's future cash flows after they have been discounted to today's value
minus the initial cost, so a positive result suggests the project adds value.
the length of time it takes for a project's net cash inflows
to repay the money first invested in it.
the idea that a sum of money is worth more now than the same sum in the future
because it can be invested to earn a return and inflation reduces its buying power.
a difference between actual and budgeted figures that reduces profit
because costs are higher than planned or revenue is lower than planned.
a financial plan that sets out the income and spending expected for a future period
which is used to guide decisions and to measure actual results.
a part of a business, such as a department, where costs can be identified and recorded
but which does not earn revenue itself.
a difference between actual and budgeted figures that increases profit
because costs are lower than planned or revenue is higher than planned.
a part of a business for which both costs and revenue can be identified
so that its profit or loss can be measured.
the difference between a budgeted figure and the actual figure
which is investigated to find out why results did not go to plan.
